caption: 妇人画像
body: 图00像是一件身份信息被部分遮蔽的人物肖像。请不要直接把它当作“看图识物”题，而是先列出3类可见证据：人物服饰与姿态、画面构图与背景、媒介/题款/收藏线索；再据此提出2个可能的作者—时代—地域组合，并用公开馆藏或艺术史资料排除其中较弱的一项。最后用一小段话说明：这幅肖像中的女性身份是被如何“制造”出来的？
rubric: 图00对应罗吉尔·凡·德·韦登《年轻女子肖像》一类早期尼德兰女性肖像：服饰与姿态证据包括高额头、透明翼状面纱、深色长袍、交叠双手和克制神情；构图与背景证据包括半身近距离构图、暗色或深蓝背景、突出面部与手部的光线，以及强调静穆与虔敬的观看关系；媒介与风格线索指向15世纪勃艮第—尼德兰宫廷肖像传统，罗吉尔·凡·德·韦登是强候选，汉斯·梅姆林等后继画家可作为较弱替代并可由馆藏归属和风格年代排除。最终结论应说明女性身份是由宫廷服饰、婚姻/贞洁符号、阶级审美和宗教化凝视共同制造出来的，而不是由肖像自然呈现出来的。

caption: 太阳辐射监测卫星一号
body: 图00给出一个空间探测/监测任务的入口材料。完成：(1) 标注图中可见的结构部件与任务暗示；(2) 查找公开资料确认发射、平台、载荷、观测对象；(3) 解释这类观测数据能服务哪些科学或业务场景。请至少给出3个URL，其中至少1个来自官方、机构或任务资料页。
rubric: 图00对应中国第一颗科学试验卫星实践一号：可见结构应归纳为近球形多面体星体、外部天线/支架和早期小型科学卫星平台特征。公开资料核验的关键事实包括1971年3月3日由长征一号在酒泉发射，卫星约221公斤、直径约1米、采用自旋稳定，任务载荷包括盖革计数器和铍窗积分电离室等探测设备。观测对象主要是高空磁场、宇宙射线、太阳X射线、辐射带粒子和空间环境参数；其数据可服务辐射带研究、空间天气预报、航天器辐射防护设计和后续空间环境监测体系建设。

caption: 恶灵古堡2：启示录
body: 从图00出发，判断它更可能属于哪一种“游戏IP改编电影”的视觉传统。请说明角色、怪物/敌对对象、武器、色调和动作姿态分别给了你什么线索；随后核验影片与原游戏系列之间的改编关系，并讨论它为什么更偏向动作片、恐怖片或科幻片中的某一种，而不是简单复刻游戏叙事。
rubric: 图00指向《生化危机：启示录》这一游戏IP改编电影的动作恐怖传统：女性战斗主角、枪械与近身战姿态、城市废墟和冷暗色调强化了动作片与末日科幻质感；怪物/敌对对象和实验失控线索则保留生存恐怖来源。改编关系上，影片并非复刻游戏流程，而是抽取《生化危机3》《代号：维罗妮卡》等游戏中的浣熊市、RPD警局、Nemesis和病毒灾变元素，并围绕原创主角Alice重组为电影叙事。因此得分点应落在“游戏视觉母题被电影类型重排”上：恐怖和科幻提供世界观，动作场面、追逐、枪战和超级化主角构成主导类型。

caption: 航天飞机
body: 说明图中飞行器系统的关键组成，并结合公开资料解释它的设计理想与实际运行结果之间的落差。回答时需要覆盖：可重复使用、任务流程、重大风险事件、退役原因。不必写成长文，但每个核心判断都要能回链到来源URL。
rubric: 图00指向航天飞机：部分可重复使用并不必然带来成本降低；设计理想与实际运行结果的最终对比 航天飞机系统由轨道器（Orbiter）、外储箱（External Tank）和两个固体火箭助推器（Solid Rocket Boosters, SRB）组成，旨在通过部分组件的重复使用来降低进入太空的成本并实现高频次发射；然而，其设计理想与实际运行结果之间存在显著落差，主要体现在可重复使用性、任务流程效率、安全风险及最终退役原因四个方面。

caption: 伊利诺伊州百年纪念半美元
body: 图00是一件“把历史纪念压缩进小型物件”的材料。请先读出可见的铭文、人物、年份、面值和象征元素；然后查证它的发行背景、设计者、发行量与材质规格。最后回答一个比较问题：纪念币上的图像叙事，与教科书式历史叙事有什么不同？
rubric: 图00指向伊利诺伊州百年纪念半美元：综上所述，1918年伊利诺伊州百年纪念半美元与教科书在真实性上的差异，本质上是功能导向的不同；5.2 互动性差异：被动接受与主动建构 在历史信息的传播与接收过程中，1918年伊利诺伊州百年纪念半美元与教科书呈现出截然不同的互动模式；例如，在探讨伊利诺伊州百年历史时，教科书可能引导学生对比不同社会群体（如移民、原住民）的经历，从而形成独立的历史解释 [来源：Step3_图像叙事与教科书叙事对比分析.；在历史信息的传播与接收过程中，1918年伊利诺伊州百年纪念半美元与教科书呈现出截然不同的互动模式。

caption: 1951年费城市政选举
body: 围绕图00重建一次20世纪中叶美国城市政治转折。你需要先判断图中人物或材料可能关联的公共职务、政党与选举场景，再查找选举结果、核心争议、改革派/机器政治的关系。输出请用“证据链”格式：图像线索 → 外部资料 → 可支持的历史解释。
rubric: 图00指向1951年费城市政选举：图像线索与历史事实的对应关系回顾 本节以新西兰总理诺曼·柯克（Norman Kirk, 1972-1974）的办公室照片（image）为视觉起点，通过象征性解读将其与20世纪中叶美国城市政治转折建立关联；政治机器衰落的结构性原因（1950s-1980s） 图像线索 → 外部资料 → 历史解释 图像线索：1970年代初的时间点（柯克任期）恰逢美国城市政治机器衰落的后期阶段；20世纪中叶美国城市政治转型的核心启示 20世纪中叶美国城市政治的转型并非单一维度的线性演进，而是传统庇护制机器政治与现代改革派治理模式在特定历史语境下的激烈博弈与结构性更替。

caption: 印第安人头像一美分硬币
body: 请把图00当作一枚硬币的“图像档案”来读：正面人物是谁或被塑造成谁？头饰、铭文、年份、花环/盾牌等元素如何组织国家身份？再检索钱币目录或官方资料，核验设计者、铸造年份、版别与材质变化。最后指出这个设计中最容易被误读的一个视觉符号。
rubric: 图00指向印第安人头像一美分硬币：文字主权与空间布局策略 在1859年印第安人头像一分硬币（Indian Head Cent）的视觉建构中，文字不仅是信息的载体，更是国家主权在微观空间内的直接宣告；通过对硬币正面图像档案（image）的分析，可以清晰地观察到设计者詹姆斯·巴顿·朗埃克（James Barton Longacre）如何利用空间布局来确立国家的权威性与边界感；人物形象的双重编码与空间平衡 硬币正面的核心视觉元素是佩戴羽毛头饰的侧面肖像；命名、视觉与传说 1859年印第安人头像一分硬币（Indian Head Cent）正面人物身份的认知偏差，是钱币收藏与公众历史记忆中一个典型的误读案例；设计背景、版别与材质核验 根据钱币目录与官方资料核验，该硬币由美国铸币局首席雕刻师 James Barton Longacre 设计，于1859年首次铸造。

caption: 肖申克的救赎
body: 图00提供的是一部电影的空间与人物氛围线索。请先不查资料，写出你从场景、光线、服装、人物关系中推断出的主题关键词；再用公开资料核验原著来源、主创、上映表现、奖项和后续口碑。最后解释：为什么有些电影的经典地位并不完全由首轮票房决定？
rubric: 图00指向肖申克的救赎：以《肖申克的救赎》为例，该片在1994年上映时面临《低俗小说》和《阿甘正传》等强片的激烈竞争，导致观众注意力分散；《肖申克的救赎》从票房失利到影史经典的逆袭路径清晰地表明：真正伟大的电影往往需要时间来证明其价值，经典地位是由长期的观众认可和文化渗透共同塑造的，而非由首映期间的商业数据所决定；普世主题的跨时空共鸣 《肖申克的救赎》之所以能从票房失利逆袭为影史经典，关键在于其触及了跨越文化、时代和年龄的普世主题 希望：影片通过安迪之口传达出“希望是美好的，也许是人间至善，而美好的事物永不消逝”的信念，成为观众在困境中的精神支柱；博弈背后的评价逻辑重构 行业奖项与公众共识的博弈，实质上是“精英审视”与“大众体验”两种评价逻辑的差异 《肖申克的救赎》的案例证明，当一部作品在首轮票房失利（北美首轮总票房2876.7万美元，低于2500万美元制作成本）且错失顶级奖项时，它依然可以通过家庭视频租赁（1995年全美最热门录像带）、电视反复播放（TNT等电视台）以及互联网时代的口碑发酵，完成从“市场失败者”到“文化经典”的身份跃迁。

caption: 执法先锋之X档案篇
body: 图00中的人物造型、动作姿态和警务/都市元素指向一种华语类型片传统。请比较它可能包含的警匪、动作、悬疑、奇案叙事成分，并检索资料确认影片身份、地区、主创与剧情梗概。要求不要只做剧情复述，而要说明类型元素怎样服务节奏、人物功能和视觉风格。
rubric: 图00指向执法先锋之X档案篇：综上所述，对峙场景作为“信息阀门”，在不同文化语境下承担着相似的节奏控制功能：在《X档案》中，它通过伪纪录片的混乱感加速感官刺激并延宕核心真相；在华语警匪片中，它通过戏剧反讽和语言博弈精密调控心理张力；在内地悬疑剧中，它则结合专业细节与身份转换，实现快节奏与深逻辑的平衡；全球类型语法的趋同与差异 基于对《X档案》“X-Cops”单集与华语警匪、悬疑及奇案类型片的比较分析，并结合图像 image 的视觉解码，可以发现全球类型片在叙事节奏、人物功能与视觉风格上呈现出显著的“语法趋同”现象，但在文化语境的具体运作机制上仍保留深刻的差异性；叙事节奏与人物功能的重构 该场景通过静态对峙蕴含动态潜能，服务于多重类型元素的融合 悬疑与奇案成分：夜间低照度环境、昏黄路灯与背景中模糊的警车闪烁，营造了黑色电影式的压抑氛围，暗示案件的非正规性或超常性质。

caption: 四大自由 (油画)
body: 图00呈现的不是单纯的家庭/公共生活场景，而是一种政治价值的视觉翻译。请选择图中2—3个最关键的视觉细节，解释它们如何把抽象理念变成日常经验；再查证相关演说、创作背景、展览/宣传或募资语境。可用表格区分：图中可见信息、外部资料支持、你的解释。
rubric: 图00指向四大自由 (油画)：下表总结了洛克威尔如何通过视觉细节实现上述三重转化，并得到外部资料的支持 这种转化逻辑在随后的战争债券募资活动中得到了验证；1943年，《星期六晚邮报》与美国财政部联合发起的“四大自由战争债券展”吸引了120万观众，筹集了超过1.32亿美元的资金；公众对画作的热烈反响表明，洛克威尔成功地将罗斯福的抽象政治理念翻译成了视觉化的生活指南，使“言论自由”不再是博物馆里的文献，而是每个观众都能在自身生活中想象和实践的经验；布斯·塔金顿（Booth Tarkington）为画作配写的文章进一步通过虚构对话揭示了言论自由的脆弱性，与画作温馨的日常场景形成张力，提醒观众这一日常实践的珍贵；作为文化符号的政治价值翻译 诺曼·洛克威尔的《言论自由》（Freedom of Speech）并非单纯描绘家庭或公共生活场景，而是将抽象的政治价值进行了视觉化的“翻译”，使其转化为可感知的日常经验。

caption: The map we need if we want to think about how global living conditions are changing
body: A distorted world map can make some questions clearer and others more dangerous. Using Images 00-02, identify what has been resized, what has been sacrificed, and what inference the viewer is invited to make. Then verify the demographic claims with open data. End with two cases: one where this visualization is the right map, and one where it is the wrong map.
rubric: Images 00–02 present population-scaled visualizations rather than ordinary geographic maps: populous regions such as Asia and future Africa are visually enlarged, while less populous but land-rich regions such as North America, Oceania, and parts of Europe are visually reduced. The sacrificed information includes land area, distance, borders, physical geography, economic weight, political power, emissions, resource use, and internal demographic nuance. The demographic claim is broadly consistent with open population data, but the intended inference is specifically about where people live and where future human welfare burdens may concentrate. This is the right map for vaccine allocation, poverty exposure, health burden, or service planning; it is the wrong map for climate responsibility, territorial control, transport distance, or geopolitical power.

caption: What do people die from in different countries?
body: Images 00-02 compare mortality patterns across places. Build a short research note with four sections: visible pattern; data source check; development-level explanation; exception or caveat. Include URLs for the mortality categories and rates you rely on, but keep chart observations separate from database claims.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to What do people die from in different countries: Temporal Trends in Infectious and Non-Communicable Diseases Analysis of Global Burden of Disease data from 1980 to 2021 reveals a distinct epidemiological transition characterized by the decline of infectious diseases and the rising burden of non-communicable conditions and medical risks [Chart observation]; World, Asia, and Europe Analysis of Global Burden of Disease data from 1980 to 2021 reveals distinct mortality divergences across the World, Asia, and Europe; The GBD study tracks death counts and rates for 371 diseases and injuries across 204 countries and territories from 1980 to 2023, utilizing data from vital registries, cancer registries, hospital records, and verbal autopsies combined with statistical modeling; Research published in Frontiers in Big Data notes that the global age-standardized death rate (ASDR) for AEMT declined by 36.

caption: More people care about climate change than you think
body: The figures suggest a gap between what people care about and what they think others care about. Explain that gap. Use the images only as the starting evidence: extract survey wording, percentages, geography, and uncertainty cues, then verify the methodology and compare with at least one other public-opinion source. Mention one way a different question wording could change the conclusion.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to More people care about climate change than you think: Validation Against Yale Program on Climate Change Communication Data To validate the observed discrepancy between personal climate concern and perceived social norms, we compare the initial survey evidence with data from the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication (YPCCC); Their "Six Americas" segmentation reveals that 52% of Americans are either "Alarmed" or "Concerned" about global warming, outnumbering the "Doubtful" and "Dismissive" segments (24%) by more than two to one; To validate the observed discrepancy between personal climate concern and perceived social norms, we compare the initial survey evidence with data from the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication (YPCCC);

caption: Increasing agricultural productivity across Sub-Saharan Africa is one of the most important problems this century
body: Using Images 00-02, explain why raising agricultural productivity in a major world region could be framed as one of this century's central development problems. Your answer should move through the evidence, but it does not need a rigid format: visible trend or gap, open-data alignment, and policy trade-off analysis. Compare at least two pathways: yield growth on existing land versus expansion of cultivated land, and explain the implications for food security, farmer incomes, and ecological costs.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Increasing agricultural productivity across Sub-Saharan Africa is one of the most important problems this century: Food Availability and Market Access Dynamics Raising agricultural productivity in major world regions is a central development challenge of this century, defined by the urgent need to balance food availability with market access while minimizing ecological costs; intensification (yield growth on existing land) and extensification (expansion of cultivated land); Balancing Food Security with Environmental Protection Raising agricultural productivity in major world regions represents one of this century's central development problems because it requires navigating a complex trade-off between meeting growing food demand and preserving ecological integrity.

caption: The end of progress against extreme poverty?
body: Do Images 00-02 support the strong claim that progress against extreme poverty is ending? Start with a provisional judgment: yes, partly, or no. Then use the visible time series, poverty line, regional shares, and post-shock changes to justify it. Check an open poverty database or methodology note, and decide whether the change is better explained by a real trend, pandemic/conflict/inflation shocks, or statistical revision.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to The end of progress against extreme poverty: The 'Partly' Verdict: Nuancing the End of Progress The available visual evidence supports a nuanced verdict of partly regarding the claim that progress against extreme poverty is ending; Evidence of Continued Progress Contrary to the notion that progress has halted, data through 2026 indicates that poverty rates continue to decline across all measured thresholds; This downward trajectory is visible across seven different poverty thresholds ranging from $3 to $40 per day, demonstrating that the mechanisms of poverty reduction remain functional; In most regions, including the Americas, Europe, Australia, and increasingly East Asia, extreme poverty rates have fallen to below 3–10%, indicating that progress has been both transformative and durable in the majority of the world;

caption: Talent is everywhere, opportunity is not. We are all losing out because of this
body: Talent is everywhere; opportunity is not. Treat Images 00-02 as clues rather than proof. What mechanisms could connect birthplace, education, migration, income, gender, and innovation? Verify at least three links with open datasets or studies, then propose one measurable intervention and one evaluation design that could test whether opportunity actually improves.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Talent is everywhere, opportunity is not. We are all losing out because of this: The visual evidence from global datasets reveals a self-reinforcing cycle where birthplace, education, income, and migration are inextricably linked to innovation capacity; This synthesis identifies three primary interconnected mechanisms that perpetuate structural inequality in opportunity; The Birthplace-Education-Innovation Nexus Birthplace acts as the initial determinant of educational access, creating a "lottery of birth" effect; The STEM Opportunity Accelerator Program (SOAP) is designed to improve opportunity for girls and young women in low-education regions by addressing three verified mechanisms: education attainment leading to innovation capacity with gender disparities, skilled migration contributing to human capital formation, and the pathway from birthplace to education and income;

caption: Technology over the long run: zoom out to see how dramatically the world can change within a lifetime
body: Images 00-02 provide material for a long-run technology diffusion investigation. Which technologies changed quickly, which changed slowly, and which turning points look like the result of falling costs, infrastructure build-out, regulatory permission, or network effects? After checking key dates and adoption rates, propose one falsifiable prediction about the diffusion of a current technology.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Technology over the long run: zoom out to see how dramatically the world can change within a lifetime: Current State and Historical Parallels The current state of electric vehicle (EV) diffusion in 2025 is characterized by significant market penetration and rapidly improving economic fundamentals; The adoption of automobiles between 1908 and 1940 illustrates a slow diffusion curve driven by mass production cost reductions; This acceleration mirrors smartphone adoption, which grew from 5% to 50% penetration in roughly five years, driven by falling costs and network effects.

caption: The world is making progress on clean water and sanitation, but is far behind its target to ensure universal access by 2030
body: Use the visual evidence to explain why clean water and sanitation can show real progress while still falling behind a 2030 target. Extract at least four facts from the figures, and find external data sources for at least two of them. End by naming the service level or region most likely to slow progress, plus one policy indicator that could be tracked over time.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to The world is making progress on clean water and sanitation, but is far behind its target to ensure universal access by 2030: In fragile contexts, safely managed drinking water coverage is 38 percentage points lower than in other countries, indicating a deep structural inability to maintain complex infrastructure; This gap is visually corroborated by regional data showing that Sub-Saharan Africa, which contains a high concentration of fragile states, exhibits 0–30% access to safely managed drinking water across most nations, with only South Africa reaching the 50–70% bracket [image]; World Bank data validates these visual estimates, reporting safely managed sanitation coverage at just 11% in Chad and 14% in the Central African Republic;

caption: Women have made major advances in politics — but the world is still far from equal
body: Images 00-02 show gains and gaps in political representation. Do three things: quantify the visible gap, verify it with an external source, and test two explanations for persistence, such as quotas, electoral systems, party gatekeeping, political violence, or social norms. Your conclusion should include one case that complicates the global-average story.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Women have made major advances in politics — but the world is still far from equal: Globally, nearly 90% of countries with 10% or fewer women in parliament use majoritarian systems, suggesting that while quotas are a powerful tool, their success is amplified when combined with electoral structures that encourage balanced party tickets; While women have made significant advances in parliamentary representation, holding approximately 23% of seats globally, they occupy only about 10–12% of executive leadership positions worldwide.

caption: Millions have died in conflicts since the Cold War; most of them in Africa and intrastate conflicts
body: Reconstruct a post-Cold War conflict-deaths narrative from Images 00-02, but be careful about data definitions. Separate regional distribution, conflict type, and death-counting rules; verify the key claims with UCDP, PRIO, or a comparable dataset; then explain why intrastate conflict or one-sided violence can dominate the statistics, and what this measurement may miss.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Millions have died in conflicts since the Cold War; most of them in Africa and intrastate conflicts: The dominance of intrastate conflict and one-sided violence in statistics highlights a shift in the nature of modern warfare, where civilian targeting and non-state actor proliferation are central; However, the reliance on fixed-base population metrics and the 25-death threshold means these measurements may miss lower-intensity violence or distort the perceived severity of conflicts in demographically dynamic regions; Interpretations of such data must therefore account for these definitional boundaries and methodological biases to avoid misleading conclusions about regional security trends;

caption: Americans See Health Care Costs, Deficit, Inflation as Big Problems Facing the Nation
body: Images 00-02 are survey charts about issue priorities in the United States. Extract the rankings, percentages, partisan gaps, and field dates, then check the survey methodology and relevant economic indicators. Finish with an explanation of no more than 200 words: why might health care costs, the deficit, and inflation all become high-salience concerns at the same time?
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Americans See Health Care Costs, Deficit, Inflation as Big Problems Facing the Nation: Rankings and Percentages of Key Concerns The April 20–26, 2026 Pew Research Center survey identifies the affordability of health care as the top economic concern, with 73% of U; While the overall population identifies health care affordability (73%), inflation (66%), and the federal budget deficit (64%) as very big problems, the intensity of these concerns varies sharply by political affiliation over time; Survey data from April 2026 reflects this convergence, with 73% of adults citing health care affordability, 66% citing inflation, and 64% citing the deficit as very big problems [image].

caption: Gas Prices Are Americans’ Top Concern in Iran War
body: Build a mechanism chain around the survey result: international event -> energy price expectations -> domestic political concern. You need to (1) identify what respondents worry about most and how groups differ, (2) verify the field dates, sample, and wording, and (3) use energy-price data or news context to judge whether the concern had a real-world trigger. Point out one place where the evidence remains thin.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Gas Prices Are Americans’ Top Concern in Iran War: The third link in the causal chain—connecting energy price expectations to domestic political concern—remains the weakest due to a lack of direct measures of political attitude change; While the chain successfully establishes that the international event caused energy price increases and that the public is aware of these increases (with 75–81% noticing price changes), the final step linking these economic expectations to substantive domestic political concern is unsupported by direct evidence; While the initial links—international conflict triggering market disruption and subsequent public awareness of price hikes—are strongly supported by evidence, the final link connecting these economic expectations to broader domestic political concern remains thin;

caption: U.S.-style birthright citizenship is uncommon around the world
body: These charts compare how one rule for acquiring citizenship is distributed around the world. First identify the classification scheme, regional differences, and exceptions; then consult legal or comparative-law sources to confirm which countries use unconditional, restricted, or mixed rules. Finally, explain how legal tradition, migration history, and state-building shape this institutional choice.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to U.S.-style birthright citizenship is uncommon around the world: Chart Interpretation and Color-Coded Categories The analysis focuses on two charts published by the Pew Research Center, titled "Birthright citizenship around the world," which utilize data from the GLOBALCIT Citizenship Law Dataset to illustrate the global distribution of jus soli (right of the soil) laws; The classification scheme divides countries into five distinct categories based on the conditions attached to birthright citizenship; These institutional choices are shaped by complex factors including legal traditions, migration histories, and state-building processes, with former colonial powers often adopting restricted models to manage post-colonial demographic changes;

caption: How Americans view racial diversity ahead of the country’s 250th anniversary
body: The chart material concerns diversity, national identity, and public attitudes. Do not just repeat the percentages; answer whether different groups are really responding to the same question. Read the overall attitude and group differences, verify the survey method and comparable demographic background, then present two explanatory models: diversity as a national advantage, and diversity as a source of political disagreement.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to How Americans view racial diversity ahead of the country’s 250th anniversary: The core thesis of this analysis posits that racial and ethnic diversity is fundamentally advantageous for the United States, serving as a driver of economic competitiveness, cultural enrichment, and democratic resilience; This perspective is strongly supported by empirical evidence from the Pew Research Center survey conducted in December 2025, which reveals a broad societal consensus on the value of diversity; adults, specifically 75%, view the nation’s demographic diversity as "good for the country," while only 10% express negative views; These findings verify that different groups are responding to the same fundamental question regarding national welfare, yet they interpret the implications through distinct lenses;

caption: What Political Issues Do Americans Hear About in Church?
body: Images 00-02 show how political issues enter religious life. Turn the issue types, hearing frequency, religious traditions, and partisan gaps into a small table; then verify the survey method and relevant research. Finally discuss when religious spaces amplify political mobilization, and when they translate political topics into moral or social-service language.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to What Political Issues Do Americans Hear About in Church: The following table summarizes the most frequently discussed issues, the percentage of attendees who hear them, and notable partisan or traditional gaps Table 1: Frequency of political issue discussions in religious services and framing patterns based on Pew Research Center data; Mobilization The interplay of these frameworks explains when religious spaces amplify political mobilization versus when they translate political topics into moral language; According to Pew Research Center data from April 2026, while only 24% of regular attendees report hearing clergy speak about the environment and 27% hear about immigration, the stance taken on these issues is highly asymmetric.

caption: Family Caregiving in an Aging America
body: Using the survey figures, assess the pressure of family caregiving in an aging society. Explain who provides care, who receives it, what time or financial costs are involved, and how those pressures transmit to employment, income, and public-policy needs. External evidence should include at least one demographic source and one long-term-care or caregiving study; end with one quantitative indicator worth tracking over the next five years.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Family Caregiving in an Aging America: The Reality of Home Care The visual evidence provided in the survey figures underscores the intimate, hands-on reality of family caregiving, depicting a younger male caregiver assisting an elderly woman with medication management in a domestic setting; A caregiver assists an elderly recipient with medication in a home environment, illustrating the personal nature of unpaid care; therefore, the assessment of caregiving pressure relies on external demographic and economic studies; Key Indicator for Future Tracking Given the diverging trends in caregiving intensity and employment stability, a critical quantitative indicator to track over the next five years is the labor force participation rate of family caregivers for individuals with dementia;

caption: Americans Are Increasingly Pessimistic About Avoiding the Worst Effects of Climate Change
body: Images 00-02 are survey evidence about public expectations for a long-term environmental risk. Extract the visible trend, partisan or demographic split, field dates, and wording cues; then check the survey methodology and compare the pattern with one external indicator or poll. Finish with a short explanation of why perceived preventability can decline even when policy concern remains high.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Americans Are Increasingly Pessimistic About Avoiding the Worst Effects of Climate Change: Image Content Analysis and Limitations The three provided images (image, image, and image) were analyzed to extract survey evidence regarding public expectations for long-term environmental risk; The Pew Research Center (May 2026) explicitly documented that "Americans are increasingly pessimistic about avoiding the worst effects of climate change," even as other metrics indicate sustained or rising concern.

caption: Teens’ Experiences on TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat
body: Using the figures as clues, reconstruct how teenagers experience several large social-media platforms. Do not just rank the apps: separate positive uses, negative encounters, algorithmic exposure, privacy or safety concerns, and group differences. Verify the survey design and include one caveat about self-reported platform experience.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Teens’ Experiences on TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat: Key topics included the frequency of use for five major platforms—YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, and Facebook—as well as teens’ perceptions of how these sites impact their mental health and sense of social connection; This design allows for an analysis that goes beyond simple usage rankings to explore positive uses, negative encounters, and algorithmic exposure.

caption: The global population pyramid: How global demography has changed and what we can expect for the 21st century
body: Images 00-02 show an age-structure story across time. Build a compact demographic reading: identify the visible shape change, infer what it implies for births, deaths, and aging, then verify the pattern with open population data. End with one forecast implication and one uncertainty that could change it.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to The global population pyramid: How global demography has changed and what we can expect for the 21st century: This time-series chart demonstrates a fundamental shape change in the global population structure; This pattern confirms that the global fertility transition is well underway, with birth numbers expected to slowly decrease after mid-century; While secondary factors such as life expectancy fluctuations due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic (which caused a 1.8-year drop in global life expectancy from 2019–2021) introduce volatility, research suggests these drops are often followed by transitory reversals and do not fundamentally alter long-term aging forecasts compared to fertility uncertainty.

caption: Why do women live longer than men?
body: The charts point to a persistent sex gap in survival. Explain the gap through a layered evidence map: visible pattern, biological or behavioral mechanisms, country-level variation, and historical change. Cite open sources for each mechanism and identify one case where the simple explanation does not fit.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Why do women live longer than men: Data from 2023 indicates that at age 65, nearly all data points lie above the line of equal mortality, demonstrating that men have higher mortality rates than women in almost every nation; Global life expectancy patterns correlate with regions where sex gaps are documented, reflecting underlying biological and behavioral mechanisms; Women in Bangladesh live 3.5 more years with disability than men (12.6 years versus 9.1 years), resulting in lower disability-free life expectancy despite their longer total lifespan.

caption: Twice as long — life expectancy around the world
body: A set of long-run survival charts suggests a major transformation in human welfare. First quantify the visible before/after contrast; then use open data to check the timing, regional spread, and remaining inequality. Conclude with a short note on why averages alone can hide very different mortality histories.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Twice as long — life expectancy around the world: The 30-Year Gap in 2023 The 2023 global landscape of human welfare is defined by a stark geographic disparity, with period life expectancy ranging from approximately 50 years in the lowest-performing regions to over 80 years in the highest Image Analysis; The time series data reveals notable inflection points, such as the sharp decline in Asian life expectancy around 1960, likely corresponding to the Great Chinese Famine, and a temporary global dip in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, followed by signs of partial recovery in 2021–2022 Image Analysis; This explains why averages alone can mask deeply different mortality histories: two populations may have similar life expectancies, yet one may achieve this through uniform longevity while the other experiences a mix of very early and very late deaths.

caption: The global decline of the fertility rate
body: Images 00-02 trace a global family-size transition. Describe the visible sequence, then test two explanations: child survival and education/income change versus contraception, policy, or norms. Use at least three URLs, and clearly separate what the figures show from what the causal evidence supports.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to The global decline of the fertility rate: Figure G31I1 establishes the necessary precondition of mortality decline, while Figures G31I0 and G31I2 illustrate the enabling role of contraceptive access and its correlation with fertility outcomes; Integrating Precondition and Proximate Causes The visual evidence presented in Figures G31I0, G31I1, and G31I2 establishes clear descriptive patterns of the global family-size transition but requires integration with external causal research to distinguish between competing explanatory frameworks; The figures alone cannot determine whether fertility decline is primarily driven by preconditions (child survival and socioeconomic change) or proximate causes (contraception, policy, and norms);

caption: Mortality in the past: every second child died
body: Read the historical child-survival figures as a shock test for modern intuitions. What does the visual evidence imply about the baseline risk children once faced? Verify the estimates with historical demographic sources, then explain which public-health or economic changes made the old pattern increasingly rare.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Mortality in the past: every second child died: Magnitude and Volatility of Pre-Modern Risk The visual evidence from historical demographic records reveals that high child mortality was not an anomaly but the baseline human condition for most of recorded history; In pre-modern societies, the magnitude of risk was catastrophic: approximately one in three children died before reaching their fifth birthday; Data from Sweden, which offers the longest continuous record starting in 1751, shows child mortality rates fluctuating between 25% and nearly 50%, with peaks around 1770–1780 where half of all newborns failed to survive to age five; Similarly, Western nations including the United States, United Kingdom, and France maintained child mortality rates around 30% during the period from 1830 to;

caption: Most international migrants don’t move very far from their home countries
body: The visual materials concern cross-border movement, but the key question is distance and geography rather than total counts. Extract the regional pattern, define what counts as an international migrant, and verify the claim with open migration data. End with one misleading interpretation that the chart could invite.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Most international migrants don’t move very far from their home countries: A fundamental distinction in migration analysis lies between migrant stocks and flows, a difference that is critical for correctly interpreting regional patterns and policy impacts; Migrant stock refers to the total number of international migrants residing in a country at a specific point in time, representing a cumulative snapshot of the population; In contrast, migrant flow measures the number of individuals who cross borders during a specific period, such as a single year, capturing the dynamic movement rather than the settled presence; However, as seen in the broader Sankey diagram analysis (image), visual volume represents migrant stock or flow magnitude, not physical distance, which can obscure the reality that most international migration is regional rather than intercontinental;

caption: It’s not just about child mortality; life expectancy increased at all ages
body: Do the figures support the claim that gains in survival occurred beyond infancy and childhood? Build your answer in three parts: visible age-specific pattern, external data check, and interpretation of which ages gained most. Include one reason why life expectancy at birth can exaggerate or understate adult survival improvements.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to It’s not just about child mortality; life expectancy increased at all ages: The analysis of survival gains reveals that improvements in life expectancy have occurred across all age groups, not merely through reductions in infant and child mortality; Visible Age-Specific Patterns and External Data Checks Historical data illustrates how reductions in infant mortality can disproportionately influence life expectancy at birth ($e0$); Why Life Expectancy at Birth Can Exaggerate or Understate Adult Survival Improvements Life expectancy at birth is an average that can distort the perception of adult survival trends for two primary reasons.

caption: Mortality in the past: every second child died
body: Images 00-02 present a historical mortality pattern that feels almost impossible from today's perspective. Explain it using a short evidence chain: figure observation -> demographic estimate -> public-health mechanism. Then name one region or period where the transition happened later and why.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Mortality in the past: every second child died: The Universal Pre-1850 Mortality Baseline The historical mortality landscape prior to 1850 presents a demographic reality that contrasts sharply with modern expectations; Analysis of long-term time series data reveals a universal baseline where child mortality was exceptionally high across all societies for which records exist; Specifically, the estimated share of newborns dying before age five consistently ranged between 25% and 35% in pre-1850 Europe and North America, meaning that historically, one in three to one in four children did not survive to their fifth birthday; Estimated share of newborns dying before age 5 (1751–2023), illustrating the universal high-mortality baseline and subsequent divergence;

caption: How do researchers study the prevalence of mental illnesses?
body: Treat these figures as a methods lesson rather than only a health chart. Explain how researchers can estimate the prevalence of conditions that are often underdiagnosed, stigmatized, or measured by surveys. Compare at least two measurement approaches and identify one source of bias that would affect cross-country comparisons.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to How do researchers study the prevalence of mental illnesses: To accurately estimate the prevalence of conditions that are often underdiagnosed or stigmatized, researchers employ two primary measurement approaches that complement administrative data; The "Iceberg" Phenomenon and Measurement Approaches To understand this bias, researchers must distinguish between two primary measurement approaches: Administrative Prevalence (passive surveillance) and Epidemiological Prevalence (active surveillance); Researchers must account for the "hidden" burden of undiagnosed cases by utilizing active surveillance methods and standardized symptom surveys, rather than relying solely on administrative records which reflect diagnostic capacity more than true prevalence.

caption: How do global statistics on suicide differ between sources?
body: The charts compare estimates of a sensitive mortality outcome across data systems. Your task is to explain why sources disagree: definitions, registration quality, modeling, stigma, and reporting incentives. Use the visuals to locate the disagreement, then cite methodological sources that justify which number you would use for a cross-country comparison.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to How do global statistics on suicide differ between sources: Comparison of Crude Rates Across Major Economies A comparison of crude suicide mortality estimates across major economies reveals significant discrepancies between data systems, driven primarily by differences in vital registration quality, methodological adjustments, and modeling approaches; The divergence is most pronounced when comparing raw reported data from the WHO Mortality Database (WHO MDB) against adjusted estimates from the WHO Global Health Estimates (GHE) and modeled figures from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation’s Global Burden of Disease (IHME GBD); This consistency suggests that high-quality civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems produce reported data that aligns closely with modeled estimates;

caption: Death rates from cardiovascular disease have fallen dramatically — what were the breakthroughs behind this?
body: Images 00-02 show a large decline in one major cause of death. Reverse-engineer the decline: identify the visible timing and countries, then test which breakthroughs plausibly mattered most, such as acute care, prevention, medications, smoking reduction, or blood-pressure control. Conclude with one remaining inequality in the trend.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Death rates from cardiovascular disease have fallen dramatically — what were the breakthroughs behind this: This confirmation is based on the explicit labeling in the provided charts and maps: image presents a global choropleth map titled "Cardiovascular disease deaths" for 2021; image displays a time-series chart explicitly labeled "Death rate from cardiovascular diseases" with age-standardized rates per 100,000 people; Global distribution of cardiovascular disease deaths in 2021, highlighting high absolute numbers in populous nations such as the USA, Russia, China, India, and Brazil; In Western developed nations (including France, Canada, Australia, the United States, and Germany), death rates have undergone a steep decline since the 1960s–1970s, dropping from baseline levels of 300–500 per 100,000 to below 100 by;

caption: Smoking: How large of a global problem is it? And how can we make progress against it?
body: Build a public-health strategy from the charts. First read the scale, trend, and geographic distribution of the risk behavior; then verify the burden estimates and policy evidence. Compare two interventions, such as taxation, advertising restrictions, cessation support, or smoke-free laws, and state what metric would show progress.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Smoking: How large of a global problem is it? And how can we make progress against it: Geographic Distribution of Smoking-Attributed Mortality The geographic distribution of smoking-attributed mortality reveals significant global disparities, with the burden of disease heavily concentrated in specific regions; Based on 2023 data from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) Global Burden of Disease study, the share of total deaths attributed to smoking varies widely, ranging from less than 3% in many low-burden areas to over 15% in high-burden hotspots; Mass media campaigns, large pictorial health warnings, and accessible cessation treatments demonstrate moderate evidence of efficacy, while advertising restrictions and youth access laws show positive but more limited effects depending on enforcement levels.

caption: If we can make maternal deaths as rare as they are in the healthiest countries, we can save almost 300,000 mothers each year
body: Images 00-02 suggest that a large number of deaths could be avoided if high-risk places reached the level of the best-performing places. Identify the gap, verify the mortality measure, and explain which health-system, transport, nutrition, or emergency-care bottlenecks are most likely involved. Include one realistic counterargument about comparability.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to If we can make maternal deaths as rare as they are in the healthiest countries, we can save almost 300,000 mothers each year: Distinguishing Share of Global Deaths from Mortality Rates The metric presented in G40I0 represents the percentage share of global maternal deaths by income group from 1985 to 2020, rather than the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR); For example, if all countries had achieved the EU-level MMR of 8 per 100,000 in 2015, global maternal deaths would have dropped from 302,700 to 11,000, indicating that approximately 290,000 deaths (a 96% reduction) were avoidable; Structural Constraints on Rapid Health System Improvement Images 00-02 suggest that a large number of deaths could be avoided if high-risk places reached the level of the best-performing places.

caption: How do researchers estimate the death toll caused by each risk factor, whether it’s smoking, obesity, or air pollution?
body: These figures ask a measurement question: how can deaths be attributed to risk factors that are not single diseases? Explain the logic of counterfactual risk assessment in plain language, then apply it to two visible risk examples. Requirements: cite a source for the method, separate exposure measurement from outcome measurement, and note one uncertainty.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to How do researchers estimate the death toll caused by each risk factor, whether it’s smoking, obesity, or air pollution: Cigarette Smoking and Lung Cancer Deaths Source Figure: image - "Cigarette sales and lung cancer mortality in the US" (1900-2010) Step 1: Definition of Exposure What is the risk factor?; , smoking cigarettes, breathing polluted air) Counterfactual World: The same people exist, but the risk factor is removed or reduced to a safe minimum level Step 2: Compare the Difference The difference in deaths between these two worlds tells us how many deaths are attributable to that risk factor;

caption: Around one-in-three children globally suffer from lead poisoning. What can we do to reduce this?
body: Images 00-02 present a widespread environmental-health exposure among children. Extract the visible scale and geography, then verify how exposure is measured and what developmental outcomes are linked to it. Finally, propose a three-part reduction plan: source control, screening, and policy enforcement.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Around one-in-three children globally suffer from lead poisoning. What can we do to reduce this: Despite this progress, lead exposure continues to cause permanent impacts on the development of the brain and nervous system, including reduced cognitive capacity, learning disabilities, and behavioral issues, with no safe threshold identified for these developmental outcomes; The data confirms that widespread environmental-health exposure among children has been significantly reduced through policy interventions implemented since the 1970s; To further reduce exposure, policy enforcement must integrate source control with rigorous screening.

caption: What is obesity and how is it measured?
body: Use the figures to explain how a health category is defined rather than simply counted. Identify the measurement rule, its thresholds, and why it is convenient; then critique it using at least two limitations, such as age, sex, body composition, ethnicity, or childhood growth standards.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to What is obesity and how is it measured: Policymakers must, however, remain aware of the inherent simplifications, such as the exclusion of body composition details in BMI or the modeling uncertainties in PAF, to avoid misinterpretation of health burdens; Both childhood (Figure 1) and adult (Figure 2) health categories rely on universal thresholds that often fail to account for significant ethnic and population-specific differences in body frame, composition, and disease risk profiles; For childhood health (Figure 1), the category is defined using Weight-for-Height Z-scores based on WHO Child Growth Standards, where children under five are classified as overweight if their metrics exceed two standard deviations above the median;

caption: Smoking: How large of a global problem is it? And how can we make progress against it?
body: The image set is an entry point to a preventable global health burden. Write a concise policy memo: scale of the problem, trend direction, two proven interventions, one political-economy obstacle, and one monitoring indicator. Keep visible chart claims distinct from external evidence.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Smoking: How large of a global problem is it? And how can we make progress against it: Geographic Distribution of Smoking-Attributable Deaths Image image presents a choropleth world map illustrating the share of total deaths attributed to smoking in 2023, utilizing data from the IHME Global Burden of Disease via Our World in Data; Global Mortality, Prevalence, and Economic Costs Tobacco use remains a leading preventable cause of death and disability worldwide, imposing a substantial burden on global health systems and economies; Trend analysis reveals a general decline in global smoking prevalence, which decreased from 22.7% in 2007 to 19.6% in 2019, and further to approximately 17% by.

caption: Our history is a battle against the microbes: we lost terribly before science, public health, and vaccines allowed us to protect ourselves
body: Images 00-02 frame human history as a struggle against infectious threats. Build a timeline from pre-modern vulnerability to modern protection, using the visuals as anchors. Then explain how sanitation, public health, antimicrobial treatment, and immunization changed the risk landscape, and where the protection remains fragile.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Our history is a battle against the microbes: we lost terribly before science, public health, and vaccines allowed us to protect ourselves: Major Infectious Killers and Mortality Patterns Before 1800 Before the 19th century, human history was defined by a profound vulnerability to infectious diseases, which acted as the primary constraint on population growth and life expectancy; Global average life expectancy in 1800 was no older than 40 years, a figure heavily skewed by extremely high infant and child mortality rates; While individuals who survived childhood could often live into their 60s or 70s, pre-modern societies universally experienced higher mortality rates at every age compared to modern standards;

caption: 17 key charts to understand the COVID-19 pandemic
body: This is a multi-chart dossier on a recent global health crisis. Choose five visible indicators and arrange them into a causal timeline: emergence, spread, burden, intervention, and recovery or inequality. Verify each indicator with open data, and flag one metric that is easy to misread.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to 17 key charts to understand the COVID-19 pandemic: This metric places COVID-19 among the leading causes of death globally for that year, reflecting the ongoing burden of the disease even after the acute phase of the pandemic; ✅ VERIFIED Metric Flagged for Misinterpretation While the indicators above are verified, R&D Funding (Indicator 1) is flagged as a metric that is easy to misread; COVID-19 was in a managed endemic phase with widespread immunity from vaccination and prior infection, whereas TB and HIV/AIDS represent chronic, ongoing burdens without recent emergence dynamics.

caption: Malaria: One of the leading causes of child deaths, but progress is possible and you can contribute to it
body: Using the charts, explain why a mosquito-borne disease can remain a leading child-health problem despite decades of progress. Your answer should connect geography, mortality burden, prevention tools, treatment, and funding. End with one concrete way an individual or institution could contribute, and one caveat about impact claims.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Malaria: One of the leading causes of child deaths, but progress is possible and you can contribute to it: Geographic Concentration in Tropical Zones The geographic distribution of mosquito-borne disease risk is heavily concentrated in tropical and equatorial zones, creating a structural barrier to global elimination; The vast spatial scope of the high-risk tropical belt makes eradication logistically and financially far more challenging than in temperate regions, reinforcing health inequalities and ensuring that mosquito-borne diseases remain a leading cause of child mortality in the Global South [image]; Climate Suitability and Structural Barriers to Eradication The persistence of mosquito-borne diseases as a leading cause of child mortality is fundamentally rooted in the intersection of environmental suitability and structural logistical challenges;

caption: More than half a million children die from diarrhea each year. How do we prevent this?
body: The figures point to a preventable cause of child mortality linked to water, sanitation, nutrition, and treatment access. Extract the visible burden and trend, then build a prevention ladder: household practice, clinical treatment, infrastructure, and vaccination or public-health programs. Support each rung with a URL.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to More than half a million children die from diarrhea each year. How do we prevent this: Current Mortality Burden by Cause (2023) In 2023, the global burden of child mortality remained heavily concentrated among preventable causes linked to water, sanitation, nutrition, and treatment access; According to the Global Burden of Disease data, neonatal conditions constituted the largest share of deaths in children under five, with preterm birth complications accounting for 623,000 deaths, neonatal asphyxia and trauma for 562,000, and neonatal sepsis and infections for 223,000 [image]; Measles, a highly vaccine-preventable disease, caused 118,000 deaths, while nutritional deficiencies directly contributed to 91,500 deaths and indirectly increased vulnerability to other infectious causes [image]; The broader global mortality landscape reflects these pediatric trends, with pneumonia causing 2.

caption: Once a leading killer, tuberculosis is now rare in rich countries — here’s how it happened
body: Images 00-02 show the decline of a once-dominant infectious killer in richer settings. Reconstruct the sequence: living conditions, public-health measures, diagnosis, antibiotics, vaccination if relevant, and surveillance. Then explain why the same disease can persist elsewhere despite the historical success story.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Once a leading killer, tuberculosis is now rare in rich countries — here’s how it happened: Global Mortality Patterns and Risk Factors Tuberculosis (TB) exemplifies a stark divergence in global health outcomes, having transitioned from a dominant infectious killer in high-income nations to a persistent crisis in low- and middle-income countries; In the Global North, including the USA, Canada, Western Europe, Australia, and New Zealand, annual TB deaths have been reduced to fewer than 100 per country; Conversely, the disease remains a massive burden in the Global South, with India recording between 30,000 and 100,000+ deaths annually, and significant mortality observed in Indonesia, Pakistan, Sub-Saharan Africa (including South Africa, Nigeria, Ethiopia, and the DRC), China, and Russia;

caption: Guinea worm disease is close to being eradicated – how was this progress achieved?
body: A near-eradication story is hidden in these visuals. Identify the intervention logic from the figures, then verify the surveillance, behavior-change, and case-containment mechanisms with open sources. Finish with a brief comparison to why some eradication campaigns are easier or harder than others.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Guinea worm disease is close to being eradicated – how was this progress achieved: Guinea Worm The comparative analysis of smallpox and Guinea worm disease reveals distinct biological and technical profiles that dictate the complexity of their respective eradication campaigns; While smallpox eradication was achieved rapidly after the introduction of intensified efforts (last natural case in 1977, declared eradicated in 1980), Guinea worm’s timeline has been extended due to the lack of a vaccine and the complexities of zoonotic transmission; The comparative analysis of smallpox and Guinea worm disease reveals distinct biological and technical profiles that dictate the complexity of their respective eradication campaigns.

caption: 数字推盘游戏
body: 围绕图00详细介绍数字推盘游戏（n-puzzle），包括其历史渊源、常见类型（如十五数字推盘和八数字推盘）、游戏规则、解法特点，以及著名的‘15-14问题’和萨姆·劳埃德的悬赏故事。
rubric: 图00指向数字推盘游戏：虽然两种游戏常被统称为“数字华容道”，但其历史起源紧密相连；萨姆·劳埃德（Sam Loyd）的角色：著名谜题专家萨姆·劳埃德后来声称自己发明了该游戏，并通过著名的“15-14 问题”悬赏故事极大地推动了游戏的普及；尽管劳埃德并未真正发明游戏，但他作为营销天才，通过这一不可能的挑战使 15-Puzzle 在全球范围内引发了热潮，使其成为历史上最著名的滑块游戏之一；在1870年代末至1880年间，十五数字推盘游戏在美国迅速传播，成为一种“瘟疫”般的社会现象；萨姆·劳埃德曾试图在美国为十五数字推盘游戏申请专利，但未能成功。

caption: How many people die from the flu?
body: How should a reader estimate mortality from a seasonal infection when surveillance, testing, and cause-of-death coding differ? Use the figures to identify the measurement problem, compare reported deaths with modeled excess mortality, and state which estimate you would use for planning a vaccination campaign.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to How many people die from the flu: Demographic Shifts and Vulnerable Populations Global demographic projections indicate a significant shift in population structure, with the population aged 65 and older projected to surpass the under-15 population between 2050 and; This trend highlights a rapidly growing vulnerable population for seasonal infections, making accurate mortality estimation increasingly critical for public health planning; Data on influenza vaccination coverage for individuals over 65 reveals massive geographic gaps, with most of Africa, Asia, and South America lacking data entirely; Core Challenges in Reporting Accuracy The figures reveal a fundamental challenge: when surveillance, testing, and cause-of-death coding differ across regions, reported deaths become unreliable indicators of true mortality burden;

caption: Pneumonia — no child should die from a disease we can prevent
body: Images 00-02 present a child-health burden that is both common and preventable. Explain the chain from pathogen exposure or infection to severe disease and death, then map interventions onto the chain: vaccination, nutrition, antibiotics, oxygen, and care access. Include one equity question the figures cannot answer alone.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Pneumonia — no child should die from a disease we can prevent: Even with vaccination programs, such as those for Hib and pneumococcus, pneumonia remains a major cause of morbidity, with incidence rates of 13.4 episodes per 1,000 child-years reported in The Gambia despite vaccination; An equity question that these figures cannot answer alone is how socioeconomic factors specifically influence the timeliness of care-seeking and the quality of diagnostic capabilities (such as pulse oximetry availability) within the households that do attempt to access care; Improving Care-Seeking Behavior and Early Recognition Improving care-seeking behavior and early recognition of childhood illness is a critical intervention point within the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) framework, targeting Stage 2 of the disease chain where initial infection manifests as early symptoms;

caption: Why are there differences between reported and estimated cases of smallpox?
body: The figures compare reported cases with reconstructed estimates for a historically important disease. Explain why administrative records can diverge from modeled estimates, especially before modern surveillance. Then use the case to discuss how historians and epidemiologists combine records, demography, and uncertainty.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Why are there differences between reported and estimated cases of smallpox: Administrative records frequently diverge from modeled estimates due to systemic inefficiencies in surveillance, particularly in historical contexts where reporting infrastructure was underdeveloped; A primary driver of this divergence is the "surveillance pyramid," where cases are lost at multiple stages: not all infected individuals develop symptoms, not all symptomatic individuals seek care, and not all diagnosed cases are reported to health authorities; For instance, in shigellosis surveillance, only about 6% of actual infections were ultimately reported to the CDC, suggesting that reported figures must be multiplied by approximately 20 to estimate true incidence;

caption: Vaccines have saved 150 million children over the last 50 years
body: Use the image set to evaluate a large claim about lives saved by a medical intervention. Break the task into: visible headline number or trend, counterfactual method, age groups affected, and uncertainty interval. Then explain why the benefit is cumulative and why it can be invisible in ordinary year-to-year charts.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Vaccines have saved 150 million children over the last 50 years: Vaccine Confidence and Public Perception (G55I0) Public perception and confidence in vaccines vary significantly across geographic regions, serving as a critical proxy for intervention effectiveness rather than a direct measure of clinical outcomes; Data from the Vaccine Confidence Project (2025) indicates that the share of respondents who "strongly agree" or "tend to agree" that vaccines are important for children ranges from 30% to 100% globally; Global map showing the share of respondents who agree that vaccines are important for children to have,; This cumulative nature explains why the full impact of vaccination programs is often invisible in ordinary year-to-year charts, which may show modest annual changes while masking the profound long-term trajectory toward eradication;

caption: What was the Golden Age of Antibiotics, and how can we spark a new one?
body: Images 00-02 are about discovery waves, resistance, and innovation incentives. Explain what made one historical period unusually productive, why the pipeline later slowed, and what would count as a credible renewal. Include scientific, regulatory, and market explanations rather than only a heroic-inventor story.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to What was the Golden Age of Antibiotics, and how can we spark a new one: Methodological Advances and Knowledge Accumulation The unusually high productivity of the Golden Age of Antibiotics (1940s–1960s) was driven by a convergence of methodological breakthroughs, accumulated basic science, and coordinated institutional structures, rather than isolated individual genius; Adaptive Regulatory Pathways and International Coordination The stagnation in antibiotic innovation following the Golden Age (1940s–1960s) cannot be attributed solely to scientific exhaustion; During the Golden Age, the regulatory environment was characterized by minimal barriers: the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act required proof of safety but not efficacy, allowing antibiotics to be approved within 1–2 years of discovery.

caption: Per capita, national, historical: how do countries compare on CO2 metrics?
body: The figures compare emissions using several denominators. Explain how the ranking changes when the unit changes: total, per-person, historical, consumption-based, or current annual emissions. Then choose which metric is fairest for three policy questions and justify each choice.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Per capita, national, historical: how do countries compare on CO2 metrics: of Fairest Metrics for Each Policy Domain Balancing Equity, Responsibility, and Practicality No single metric can capture the full complexity of climate justice; Hybrid Approach – Historical Cumulative Emissions (60%) + Current Economic Capacity (40%) For allocating financial contributions to global climate funds, historical cumulative emissions provide the strongest moral foundation, as climate change is driven by accumulated atmospheric CO₂ rather than annual flows; Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAM) Recommended Metric: Production-Based Current Annual Emissions with Consumption-Based and Development Adjustments For trade policy, production-based current annual emissions are the necessary operational foundation because they are measurable at the border and prevent carbon leakage;

caption: What is the ozone layer, and why is it important?
body: Treat the visuals as a primer on an atmospheric shield. Explain what is being protected, what damaged it, how the damage was detected, and what policy response changed the trajectory. Then identify one lesson for climate or pollution governance, and one limit of the analogy.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to What is the ozone layer, and why is it important: Humans and UV-B Radiation The atmospheric shield, specifically the stratospheric ozone layer located between 15 and 35 kilometers in altitude (peaking at 20–25 km), serves a critical protective function for life on Earth; This "good ozone" is distinct from tropospheric ozone found near the surface (0–15 km), which acts as a local air pollutant with negative impacts on human respiratory health; Vertical distribution of atmospheric ozone, distinguishing between harmful tropospheric pollution and essential stratospheric UV protection; The integrity of this shield was compromised by the release of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other ozone-depleting substances, leading to severe thinning of the ozone layer;

caption: The world’s energy problem
body: The image set presents an energy dilemma. Turn it into a two-axis analysis: energy access and environmental impact. Use the figures to identify the trade-off, verify the data with open sources, and compare two pathways for resolving it without assuming that demand simply disappears.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to The world’s energy problem: Together, these three images define the energy dilemma; Resolving this trade-off requires pathways that expand energy access (lowering indoor pollution deaths) without proportionally increasing fossil fuel consumption (limiting CO₂ emissions), necessitating a massive scale-up in renewable energy and efficiency improvements rather than a simple reduction in demand; The Optimal Strategy for Global Equity The analysis of the energy dilemma reveals that neither supply-side transformation nor demand-side efficiency alone can resolve the tension between expanding energy access and mitigating environmental impact.

caption: Low-carbon technologies need far less mining than fossil fuels
body: Images 00-02 compare material requirements across energy systems. Extract the visible quantities and units, then test the claim against a fossil-fuel baseline and a lifecycle perspective. Include at least one caveat about mineral type, geography, recycling, or supply-chain risk.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Low-carbon technologies need far less mining than fossil fuels: Detailed extraction from low-carbon technology assessments shows significant variation in material needs, measured in kilograms per gigawatt-hour (kg/GWh) [Image: image]; When testing claims against a fossil-fuel baseline, it is noted that while low-carbon technologies have higher upfront material intensities per unit of capacity, lifecycle assessments indicate they generally require far less mining overall compared to the continuous fuel extraction needed for fossil fuel systems; Construction Phase Material Intensity Comparison A comparison of construction-phase material intensity reveals significant variation across energy technologies, challenging the notion that low-carbon systems universally require substantially more materials than fossil fuel counterparts;

caption: The world has become more resilient to disasters, but investment is needed to save more lives
body: The charts suggest that societies have become better at surviving disasters, but not that disasters no longer matter. Explain the difference between hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and deaths. Verify the visible trend, then state what kind of investment would reduce deaths further and what metric would prove it.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to The world has become more resilient to disasters, but investment is needed to save more lives: Early Warning Systems and Last-Mile Communication Early Warning Systems (EWS) represent a critical investment area for reducing disaster mortality, yet significant gaps in coverage and effectiveness remain; Currently, approximately one-third of the world's population, predominantly in the poorest countries, lacks access to multi-hazard early warning systems; While progress has been made—with more than 60% of all countries now reporting having such systems, more than double the number from 2015—the primary challenge has shifted from detection to dissemination; Data indicates a significant decline in average disaster-related mortality, demonstrating that societies have become more resilient and better at surviving disasters through improved preparedness, early warning systems, and infrastructure resilience.

caption: Living Planet Index: what does it really mean?
body: A biodiversity index is shown declining, but the interpretation is not straightforward. Explain what the index measures, what it does not measure, and why population-weighted changes can be misunderstood as species extinctions. Use the figures plus methodological sources to produce a careful reading.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Living Planet Index: what does it really mean: Analysis of LPI Charts (G62I0-G62I2) The Living Planet Index (LPI) serves as a key indicator of the state of global biological diversity, tracking changes in vertebrate wildlife populations over time; Living Planet Index trends from 1970 to 2020, showing the central estimate and confidence intervals based on WWF and ZSL data; Cluster Decline The Living Planet Index (LPI) presents a stark visual narrative of biodiversity loss, with the central estimate declining from a baseline of 100% in 1970 to approximately 27% in.

caption: You want to reduce the carbon footprint of your food? Focus on what you eat, not whether your food is local
body: The figures ask whether food choices or food miles matter more for dietary emissions. Extract the visible comparison, then verify it with lifecycle assessment sources. Conclude with a practical decision rule for consumers and one exception where transport or production method changes the answer.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to You want to reduce the carbon footprint of your food? Focus on what you eat, not whether your food is local: The Minimal Role of Transport in Total Emissions Transport plays a surprisingly minor role in the total greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of the global food system; Comprehensive lifecycle assessments indicate that transport accounts for only 5% of global food system emissions; for instance, a study of average American households found that food transport contributed just 5% (approximately 0.4 tonnes CO₂eq) to total household food emissions; A practical decision rule for consumers is that substituting less than one day per week’s worth of calories from red meat and dairy with chicken, fish, eggs, or plant-based alternatives achieves greater GHG reductions than buying all food from local sources;

caption: How many animals get slaughtered every day?
body: Images 00-02 quantify animal slaughter at a scale that is hard to imagine. Convert the visual evidence into rates, species composition, and regional or dietary drivers. Then discuss one ethical, environmental, or data-quality question that the raw counts alone cannot settle.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to How many animals get slaughtered every day: Land Animal Slaughter Trends (image) The global slaughter of land animals for meat has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past six decades, characterized by an exponential increase in total numbers and a profound shift in species composition; Data from 1961 to 2024 reveals that the annual number of land animals slaughtered has risen from approximately 7 billion to nearly 80 billion; Yearly number of animals slaughtered for meat worldwide, 1961–2024; Ethical and Data-Quality Implications While images such as image provide precise annual slaughter counts, they cannot settle ethical questions regarding animal welfare conditions, suffering during slaughter, or the moral status of different species;

caption: Global deforestation peaked in the 1980s. Can we bring it to an end?
body: The charts show a long-run land-use transition. Identify the peak, regional shifts, and drivers; then verify the trend with forest-change data. Finish with a policy scenario: what would have to happen for the decline to continue, and what could reverse it?
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Global deforestation peaked in the 1980s. Can we bring it to an end: planted) matters beyond simple area metrics Acknowledging country-level heterogeneity within regional trends Understanding that recent slowdown in decline rate warrants continued vigilance This cross-referenced foundation provides solid basis for developing policy scenarios in Steps 6-7 analyzing what conditions would sustain the declining trend and what interventions could reverse it; 1700 at 61 million km² (G65I1) Deforestation rate peak: 1980s-early 1990s at 151 million ha net loss (G65I2) Temperate deforestation peak: First half of 20th century (G65I2) Regional Shifts Northern regions (Europe, Russia, N; The declining trend in global deforestation since the 1980s-1990s peak is not inevitable or irreversible.

caption: Where does the plastic in our oceans come from?
body: Use the figures to trace a pollution pathway from production or waste management to rivers and oceans. Extract the geographic pattern, verify the estimated flows, and distinguish between coastal waste, river transport, fishing gear, and high-income consumption. End with one intervention targeted at the dominant pathway.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Where does the plastic in our oceans come from: Integrated Triple-Threat Regions The dominant pollution pathway is identified as river transport originating from high-population coastal and monsoon regions in Southeast Asia; In these areas, massive population-driven consumption combines with specific geographic factors, including heavy rainfall, dense river networks, and proximity to the coast, to create an extremely high risk of ocean emissions; Indonesia and the Philippines represent the most critical risk levels, combining mismanaged waste volumes exceeding 1 million tonnes and 100,000–1 million tonnes respectively, with ocean entry probabilities greater than 10%;

caption: Around one-in-three children globally suffer from lead poisoning. What can we do to reduce this?
body: This is another entry point into childhood exposure to an environmental toxin. Instead of repeating the headline scale, compare two measurement strategies and two mitigation strategies. Which populations are hardest to observe, and which intervention would produce the quickest measurable reduction?
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Around one-in-three children globally suffer from lead poisoning. What can we do to reduce this: Optimal Measurement Frameworks The optimal measurement framework for assessing childhood environmental toxin exposure requires the sequential integration of two distinct strategies: biomonitoring and environmental media sampling; Prioritizing High-Impact Interventions To address childhood exposure to environmental toxins effectively, it is essential to move beyond headline-scale assessments and instead evaluate specific measurement and mitigation strategies; The analysis identifies which populations remain most difficult to observe and determines which intervention yields the quickest measurable reduction in exposure levels.

caption: Access to basic education: almost 60 million children of primary school age are not in school
body: Images 00-02 present an education-access gap. Identify who is out of school, where the gap is concentrated, and how it has changed over time. Then verify the counts with open education data and propose one policy lever, one implementation barrier, and one outcome metric.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Access to basic education: almost 60 million children of primary school age are not in school: The "time compression" effect suggests that policy interventions in the mid-to-late 20th century were highly effective in accelerating literacy gains in countries like China and Mexico; However, the static 2024 data for pre-primary and primary education reveals that the frontier of exclusion has shifted geographically to Sub-Saharan Africa and conflict-affected states, where structural barriers continue to impede access despite global progress; The remaining 20–30% illiteracy rate in India and Egypt underscores that while massive gains have been made, the final mile of universal education access remains a significant challenge; Alignment with Policy Goals and Equity The proposed policy of school fee abolition aligns directly with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 4.

caption: The Internet's history has just begun
body: The figures frame a communication technology as early in its historical arc. Compare adoption curves, infrastructure constraints, and inequality in access. Then make a falsifiable claim about what would indicate maturation rather than continued early-stage expansion.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to The Internet's history has just begun: Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations theory, originally published in 1962 and updated through 1995, provides a foundational framework for understanding how new technologies spread by categorizing adopters into five distinct segments based on their innovativeness; Early Adopters (13.5%), who serve as influential opinion leaders triggering the steep upward slope of adoption; the Early Majority (34%), who are pragmatic and wait for proven success; Maturation of a technology is indicated by specific structural shifts rather than continued early-stage expansion; In the context of the communication technology analyzed, the current adoption trajectory suggests an early position in its historical arc, characterized by significant infrastructure constraints and notable inequality in access.

caption: Scaling up: how increasing inputs has made artificial intelligence more capable
body: Images 00-02 show a scaling relationship in machine learning. Explain the visible link between compute, data, model size, benchmark performance, or capability. Then verify the technical claim with open sources and discuss two constraints: cost/energy and evaluation reliability.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Scaling up: how increasing inputs has made artificial intelligence more capable: Data Size and Benchmark Performance The relationship between training data volume and model capability is characterized by a strong positive correlation, where increased dataset size generally leads to higher performance on knowledge benchmarks such as the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) test; As illustrated in the scatter plot below, this relationship follows a logarithmic scaling pattern, meaning that exponentially more data is required to achieve linear gains in benchmark scores; Relationship between training dataset size (tokens) and MMLU benchmark performance across various AI models; GPT-4, trained on over 10 trillion tokens, achieves an MMLU score of approximately 86–87%, approaching expert human performance levels of 87–88%; economic cost and evaluation reliability.

caption: Tracking global data on electric vehicles
body: Use the charts to reconstruct a market transition in road transport. Extract sales shares, regional leaders, and inflection points; then verify the data and explain which forces are most plausible: policy, battery costs, charging infrastructure, model availability, or fuel prices.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to Tracking global data on electric vehicles: Overview of Source Charts and Data Extraction The analysis of the market transition in road transport is based on three primary source files: image, image, and image; The core quantitative data is derived from image and its duplicate image, which present identical line charts titled "Share of new cars sold that are electric, 2010 to 2025"; These charts, sourced from the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook 2026 and published by Our World in Data, define electric vehicles as comprising both fully battery-electric (BEV) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEV); Share of new cars sold that are electric across six regions from 2010 to; the World average, Norway, the United Kingdom, the European Union (27), China, and the United States.

caption: HPV vaccination: How the world can eliminate cervical cancer
body: The image set links vaccination coverage to a cancer-prevention goal. Explain the causal chain from infection prevention to disease elimination, verify the coverage and burden figures, and identify the threshold or implementation gap that determines whether elimination is realistic.
rubric: Images 00–02 point to HPV vaccination: How the world can eliminate cervical cancer: Biological Mechanism of Carcinogenesis The progression from HPV infection to cervical cancer follows a well-defined, multi-stage pathway that typically takes 10-20 years; HPV Infection (Acute Phase) Sexually transmitted carcinogenic HPV infection occurs, most commonly in adolescence and early adulthood; HPV16 is the most important type, responsible for approximately 40% of high-grade lesions and 50% of cervical cancers, despite causing only 20% of infections; Official Health Statistics The analysis of the causal chain from infection prevention to disease elimination reveals that while HPV vaccination is a critical primary prevention tool, current global coverage levels present significant challenges to meeting elimination targets;
